overview: This map label covers Sri Lanka from 800 to 900, especially the Anuradhapura monarchy and the communities, monasteries and ports around it. It is one century within a much longer history, not the lifetime of a single dynasty. The coarse island outline clips parts of the coastline and does not demonstrate equal royal control everywhere. Royal and monastic claims to land and labour could compete. Earlier Simhala and the much later Sinhalese-kingdom records have separate cards or map entries.

periods.title: Ninth-century Anuradhapura and regional communities
periods.summary: Kings, monasteries and local communities negotiated authority over land and resources, while the island remained connected to southern India and ocean trade.

items.text: Sena I’s reign included a damaging Pandyan raid from southern India. A later inscription identifies this ruler, using his title Salamevan, as the founder of Ritigala monastery. The combination of inscription and chronicle places renewed royal patronage after the raid. Scholars use different absolute chronologies for these kings, so a precise modern year should not be invented from a regnal title alone.

Under Sena II, an army departed through Mahatittha, now called Mantai, for a campaign in the Pandyan kingdom. The same harbour could receive merchandise or launch a military expedition. Historian Wijerathne Bohingamuwa cautions that chronicles emphasize warfare, so archaeology is essential for understanding the port’s less dramatic but persistent commercial work.

A rough pillar at Viyaulpata records privileges for a monastic dwelling, issued by the heir-apparent Mahinda in Sena II’s first regnal year. Two officers, Kaṇṇā and Rāvaṇā, assembled local notables before setting up the pillar and proclaiming the order. A written command also needed people to hear about it; carving a stone was only part of making government work.

Inscriptions from the Sigiriya-Dambulla area, dated from the middle of the ninth century into the tenth, describe competing claims over fields, water, labour and produce. Monasteries could control substantial resources, while royal officials intervened in those arrangements. For farming households, an endowment could change who claimed their work or part of their harvest.

Dry-zone communities stored seasonal rain in large reservoirs and smaller, gravity-fed chains of tanks. Canals linked these supplies with settlements and fields. This infrastructure had developed over generations before the ninth century. Maintaining it connected people’s farming work with the wider landscape.

Anuradhapura’s early medieval residential layers contain shallow, internally grooved bowls called nambiliya. Researchers associate them with separating grit from rice. Their increasing presence suggests more city residents were processing rice themselves as supply networks changed. Those grooves helped keep unwanted crunch out of dinner.

Excavations at Mantai recovered ninth-century Changsha pottery from China alongside locally made wares and other imports. A broken bowl can therefore connect an island port to kilns thousands of kilometres away. Its arrival need not mean that a Chinese potter or merchant lived in the particular house where it was eventually discarded.

Mantai’s deposits, spanning the early centuries CE into medieval times, contain rice, wheat, pulses and millets. Researchers think much of the rice reached the port in its husk, while wheat arrived already cleaned, probably through trade. These finds reveal provisioning and varied food traditions across several centuries; they are not a single ninth-century household’s shopping list.

Microscopic plant remains at Mantai point to the importance of palms. The excavators interpret their abundance as evidence for palm leaves used in buildings, and suggest fibres could also have supplied ropes for boats and port work. A palm could contribute to shelter and transport as well as food, although each proposed use leaves different amounts of archaeological evidence.

Sri Lankan gold kahavanu circulated between roughly the eighth and eleventh centuries. Their designs show a standing figure on one side and a seated figure on the other, with a short Nagari inscription. Scholars have proposed several readings of that legend. These coins are surviving evidence for skilled metalworking and exchange, without telling us how many coins an ordinary family possessed.

sections.title: Living, bathing and learning in monasteries

items.text: The Western Monasteries near Anuradhapura and related sites such as Ritigala contain paired stone platforms linked by a narrow gangway. Rear platforms preserve evidence of roofs, partitions and doorways; front platforms were generally open. Scholars associate this architecture with communities devoted to meditation. The surviving arrangement helps distinguish a place to live from an open area used for other activities.

These monastic complexes also had paths interpreted as meditation walkways and buildings for hot-water bathing. Bathhouses could include a fireplace, water containers and seats. The remains make monastic life more tangible: thought and teaching took place in bodies that also needed washing, rest and movement. The larger complexes shared some facilities among several residential units.

Some monastic urinals were unexpectedly fancy. Carved stone slabs had foot supports, a collecting depression and an outlet, with architectural decoration showing a building. Separate latrines could be plainer and farther from the living rooms. Why decorate a urinal so elaborately? Scholars disagree about the symbolism, but the practical need is easy to recognize.

The hospital at Mihintale is dated to the ninth century through its inscriptional and archaeological context. Rooms opened onto an inner courtyard and are interpreted as accommodation for patients. The outer area included a refectory and spaces associated with preparing and storing medicines. Caring for sick people required food, supplies and organized space as well as a healer.

Mihintale also preserves a stone trough hollowed into a shape that fits a human body, interpreted as a medical bath. It is one of the objects helping identify the site as a hospital. The trough shows that treatment could involve immersion; it cannot by itself establish which ingredients were used for every patient or how effective a treatment was.

A short ninth-century Sinhala phrase from the Kivulekada inscription is transcribed “Riṭgal-aram kärū Salamevan Rajpahi”, referring to King Salamevan as the builder of Ritigala monastery. These are scholarly Latin letters representing the inscription’s language, rather than a reproduction of its carved Sinhala letters. A royal title and a building project help scholars identify Sena I behind the name.

A medieval visitor to Sigiriya left a wonderfully human note. Nimal de Silva transcribes its opening as “Budalmi”, meaning “I am Budal”. Budal explained that so many people had already written songs that he did not write one. He wrote to explain why he was not writing a poem. His individual date is uncertain within the broader medieval graffiti tradition.

Sigiriya’s graffiti preserve visitors’ names, places, titles and responses to its paintings. Scholars have read both polished poems and much shorter notes. They reveal people choosing words for an audience, not merely copying a royal command. The surviving writers were a selected literate group, so their words cannot measure how many children elsewhere learned to read.

The Kivulekada inscription nearly had a second career holding up a granary. When it was recorded in 1892, a local official said he had dug out the slab to use as a support. A researcher visiting in 1928 found it half-buried with its writing face down. Ordinary reuse helped determine which clues later archaeologists could find.

ending.text: The map stops at 900, before Anuradhapura lost its role as the chief capital. Chola conquest changed the political landscape around the end of the tenth century; UNESCO dates a destructive attack to 993. Polonnaruwa became a successor capital, preserving monuments from Chola and later Sri Lankan rulers. Political institutions changed while communities and religious traditions continued.
